source.title: Gluconeogenesis & the Control of Blood Glucose
source.section: Gluconeogenesis and the regulation of blood glucose levels through the synthesis of glucose from noncarbohydrate precursors.

chunks.text: Gluconeogenesis is the process of synthesizing glucose from noncarbohydrate precursors. The major substrates for gluconeogenesis are glucogenic amino acids, lactate, glycerol, and propionate. The liver and kidney are the major gluconeogenic tissues. The liver is the primary gluconeogenic organ. The renal cortex of the kidney may contribute about 10% of whole body gluconeogenesis after a short-term fast of 18 to 24 hours. The kidney is not a net source of glucose because the renal medulla is a consumer of glucose. With long-term fasting of about 7 days, the kidney can supply net glucose carbon to contribute to glucose homeostasis. The key gluconeogenic enzymes are expressed in the small intestine. Propionate from intestinal bacterial fermentation of carbohydrates is a substrate for gluconeogenesis in enterocytes. The intestine is not a net consumer of lactate and alanine or glycerol, the major substrates for gluconeogenesis. The intestine is a consumer of glucose in the fasting state. Any glucose synthesis that occurs locally in the intestine is metabolized locally.

chunks.text: Throughout the 24-hour feeding fasting cycle, gluconeogenic precursors are available. In the fasting state, adipose tissue lipolysis releases glycerol. In the fasting state, skeletal muscle releases lactate. In the fasting state, skeletal muscle releases gluconeogenic amino acids. As the fast is extended, glycerol provides an increasing role in supplying carbon for gluconeogenesis. As the fast is extended, amino acids provide an increasing role in supplying carbon for gluconeogenesis. Glucose demands of peripheral tissues, including the brain, decrease as a fast progresses. The decrease in glucose demand helps preserve vital protein stores. In the fed state, gluconeogenic supply does not decrease; it is elevated. In the fed state, glycerol supply decreases due to decreased lipolysis. In the fed state, lactate supply does not decrease primarily because of high rates of glycolysis in skeletal muscle. In the fed state, amino acid supply increases as amino acids derived from dietary protein are delivered directly into the portal vein. During exercise, lactate supply from working muscle supports the increased gluconeogenic demand of exercise.

chunks.text: The transport and uptake of amino acids, glycerol, and lactate are regulated differently. The liver is extremely efficient at taking up glycerol. More than 60% of glycerol delivered to the liver is removed on first pass. More than 60% of glycerol delivered to the liver is removed on first pass remains constant in response to changes in insulin, glucagon, and epinephrine. Amino acid removal is very sensitive to glucagon and to a lesser extent insulin. Glucagon is a potent stimulator of the transport of glucogenic amino acids by the liver. About 20% of these amino acids are removed on first pass. First pass extraction can increase to more than 60% in the presence of an increase in glucagon. Insulin can stimulate amino acid transport, but the response is much smaller than that of glucagon. Lactate uptake by the liver is complex because the liver can produce lactate during high rates of glycogen breakdown. In the fasting state, the primary driver of lactate uptake is the availability of lactate. When lactate is increased along with increases in glucagon, the liver can become an efficient consumer of lactate, supporting the gluconeogenic response, for example, as seen in exercise.

chunks.text: In disease states associated with hyperglycemia, such as infection and diabetes, gluconeogenesis is inappropriately increased. In critically ill patients, in response to injury and infection, gluconeogenic supply is very high. Elevated lactate, increased lipolysis, and increased protein catabolism contribute to the high gluconeogenic supply in critically ill patients. Underlying insulin resistance and high glucagon levels drive gluconeogenesis in critically ill patients. Hyperglycemia is associated with poor outcomes in critically ill patients. In insulin deficiency, as seen in diabetic ketoacidosis in type 1 diabetes, unopposed lipolysis and protein catabolism amplify hyperglycemia. Hyperglycemia leads to changes in osmolality of body fluids. Hyperglycemia leads to impaired blood flow. Hyperglycemia leads to intracellular acidosis. Hyperglycemia leads to increased superoxide radical production. Changes in osmolality, blood flow, intracellular acidosis, and superoxide radical production result in deranged endothelial and immune system function. Changes in osmolality, blood flow, intracellular acidosis, and superoxide radical production lead to impaired blood coagulation.

chunks.text: With liver failure, gluconeogenesis is impaired. With liver failure, hypoglycemia develops. Liver failure occurs despite high substrate supply, severe insulin resistance, and very high glucagon levels. The inability to support energy production in the liver starves the gluconeogenic pathway of the energy required to support the synthesis of glucose. The inability to support energy production in the liver is due to impaired citric acid cycle flux and ureagenesis.

Propionate is a major precursor of glucose in ruminants. Propionate enters gluconeogenesis via the citric acid cycle. Propionyl-CoA is carboxylated to D-methylmalonyl-CoA. chunks.text: Phosphofructokinase-1 regulates glycolysis and is subject to feedback control. Phosphofructokinase-1 is inhibited by citrate and normal intracellular concentrations of ATP. Phosphofructokinase-1 is activated by 5′AMP. At normal intracellular [ATP], the enzyme is about 90% inhibited. The inhibition of phosphofructokinase-1 by ATP is reversed by 5′AMP. 5′AMP acts as an indicator of the energy status of the cell. When ATP is used in energy-requiring processes, resulting in the formation of ADP, [AMP] increases. A relatively small decrease in [ATP] causes a several fold increase in [AMP]. [AMP] acts as a metabolic amplifier of a small change in [ATP], serving as a sensitive signal of the energy state of the cell. The activity of phosphofructokinase-1 is regulated in response to the energy status of the cell to control the quantity of carbohydrate undergoing glycolysis prior to its entry into the citric acid cycle. AMP activates glycogen phosphorylase, increasing glycogenolysis. The inhibition of phosphofructokinase-1 by ATP leads to an accumulation of glucose-6-phosphate. The accumulation of glucose-6-phosphate inhibits further uptake of glucose in extrahepatic tissues by inhibiting hexokinase. Glucokinase, present in the liver, is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate. This allows for high rates of glucose entry and diversion to glycogen deposition. Gluconeogenesis-derived carbon can be diverted to glycogen as well.

PFKFB3 has a ratio of over 500, biasing it to have high kinase activity. PFKFB3 expression biases cells to high rates of glycolysis. PFKFB3 is expressed in the placenta and is induced in cancer cells.

chunks.text: Glycolysis and glycogen metabolism involve a cycle of phosphorylation and dephosphorylation. Glucokinase and glucose-6-phosphatase are part of this cycle. Phosphofructokinase-1 and fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase are part of this cycle. Pyruvate kinase, pyruvate carboxylase, and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase are part of this cycle. Glycogen synthase and phosphorylase are part of this cycle. Opposing enzymes in glycolysis and gluconeogenesis are regulated to prevent cycling between phosphorylated and nonphosphorylated intermediates. Cycling would lead to net hydrolysis of ATP. In the liver, futile cycling of carbon occurs at a low rate of 1-2%. Futile cycling of carbon allows the liver to rapidly transition between fed, fasted, or exercising states.

In the postabsorptive state, the concentration of blood glucose is maintained between 4.5 and 5.5 mmol/L. After the ingestion of a carbohydrate meal, the concentration of blood glucose may rise to 6.5 to 7.2 mmol/L. In starvation, the concentration of blood glucose may fall to 3.3 to 3.9 mmol/L.

A sudden decrease in blood glucose causes convulsions because of the brain's dependence on glucose. Much lower concentrations of blood glucose can be tolerated if hypoglycemia develops slowly enough for adaptation to occur.

The blood glucose level in birds is considerably higher, at 14 mmol/L. In ruminants, the blood glucose level is considerably lower, at approximately 2.2 mmol/L in sheep and 3.3 mmol/L in cattle.

Ruminants ferment virtually all dietary carbohydrate to short-chain fatty acids. These short-chain fatty acids largely replace glucose as the main metabolic fuel of the tissues, including the brain, in the fed state.

The digestible dietary carbohydrates yield glucose, galactose, and fructose. Glucose, galactose, and fructose are transported to the liver via the hepatic portal vein. Galactose is readily converted to glucose in the liver. Fructose is readily converted to glucose in the liver.

Glucose is formed from two groups of compounds that undergo gluconeogenesis: those that involve a direct net conversion to glucose, including most amino acids and propionate. Glucose is formed from two groups of compounds that undergo gluconeogenesis: those that are the products of the metabolism of glucose in tissues. Lactate is formed by glycolysis in skeletal muscle and erythrocytes. Lactate is transported to the liver and kidney where it reforms glucose. The process of lactate being transported to the liver and kidney where it reforms glucose is known as the Cori cycle, or the lactic acid cycle (Figure 19-4).

In the fasting state, there is a considerable output of alanine from skeletal muscle. Alanine is formed by transamination of pyruvate produced by glycolysis of muscle glycogen. Alanine is exported to the liver. In the liver, alanine is transaminated back to pyruvate. Pyruvate is a substrate for gluconeogenesis in the liver. The glucose-alanine cycle provides an indirect way of utilizing muscle glycogen to maintain blood glucose in the fasting state. The glucose-alanine cycle carries nitrogen derived from oxidized amino acids by the muscle to the liver for ureagenesis (see Figure 19–3).

Glycerol released by adipose tissue is another source of gluconeogenic carbon along with the lactate released by muscle. The ATP required for the hepatic synthesis of glucose from pyruvate or glycerol is formed by the oxidation of fatty acids derived from adipose tissue lipolysis. Glucose is also formed from liver glycogen by glycogenolysis (see Chapter 18).

chunks.text: The maintenance of a stable blood glucose concentration is one of the most finely regulated of all homeostatic mechanisms. The regulation involves the liver, extrahepatic tissues, and several hormones. Liver cells are freely permeable to glucose in either direction via the GLUT 2 transporter. Cells of extrahepatic tissues, apart from pancreatic β-islets, are relatively impermeable to glucose. Unidirectional glucose transporters in extrahepatic tissues are regulated by insulin in insulin-sensitive tissues such as muscle, heart, and adipose tissue. Transport from the bloodstream is an important determinant of glucose utilization in extrahepatic tissues, but it is not the sole determinant. The role of various glucose transporter proteins found in cell membranes is shown in Table 19–2.

chunks.text: Hexokinase acts at a constant rate under all normal conditions in the liver. Hexokinase ensures an adequate rate of glycolysis to meet the liver’s needs. Glucokinase has a lower affinity for glucose compared to hexokinase. The activity of glucokinase increases with an increase in the concentration of glucose in the hepatic portal vein. Gluconeogenesis is the process of synthesizing glucose or glycogen from noncarbohydrate precursors. It is of particular importance when carbohydrate is not available from the diet. The main substrates are amino acids, lactate, glycerol, and propionate.
The pathway of gluconeogenesis in the liver and kidney utilizes those reactions in glycolysis that are reversible plus four additional reactions that circumvent the irreversible nonequilibrium reactions.
Since glycolysis and gluconeogenesis share the same pathway but operate in opposite directions, their activities are regulated reciprocally.
Insulin is secreted as a direct response to hyperglycemia; it stimulates the liver to store glucose as glycogen and increases uptake of glucose into extrahepatic tissues.
Glucagon is secreted as a response to hypoglycemia and activates both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver, causing release of glucose into the blood.
